paragraphs.text:
Christian Propositions Addressed to the [?]

Everything that comes into being from some underlying subject comes into being by nature, by art or by choice. By nature, as a human being from a human being, and wheat from wheat. By art, as garments from weaving and houses from building. By choice, as the universe from [?] what was before. Moreover, many different and contrary natures do not come into being from any single nature. For example, an ox and bronze, water, fire and nuts do not come into being from human nature. In the same way, different and contrary materials do not come into being from any single art, since the art is something other than the material that is reshaped by it. For example, wool does not come into being from the art of weaving. Rather, weaving refashions wool that already exists, and is itself something other than the wool. And that from choice not only do contrary natures not come into being, but natures do not come into being at all, [?]

1. This being so, do the things that come into being from matter come into being by nature, by art or by choice? If by nature, how can many different and contrary natures come into being from matter when it is one? If by art, then first, who is the artisan? For no one is artisan and matter at the same time. And second, how could many different and contrary natures have come into being from one matter by the procedure of an art? But if the things that come into being from matter come into being neither by nature, nor by choice, nor by art, tell us how the things from matter come into being.

2. Everything that comes into being from some underlying subject comes into being by nature, by art or by choice. If, then, the differences and contrary natures of existing things have come into being neither by nature, nor by art, nor by choice, how have the natures of existing things come into being from some underlying subject? But if the natures of existing things have not come into being from some underlying subject, tell us where the natures of existing things have come from.

3. If God is in a place as to his essence, how is God not circumscribed in his essence? And if God is circumscribed in his essence, how is God all-knowing in his essence? How is God God in his essence? 4. If God is circumscribed in what he is but uncircumscribed in quantity, how are God's quantity and what he is the same thing? But if they are not, how could it
be said that the various names and terms used of God signify one thing, because of the oneness and simplicity of his essence?

5. Suppose nothing separates the two principles, but they lie side by side like light and shadow, or as the sun lies beside every body without being in it, mixed with it or blended with it. Then first, how will the better principle not be the cause of the worse one's existence, as light is the cause of shadow [?]? And second, how will the worse principle not benefit from the better, as [bodies benefit from] the sun

6. Suppose the Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit is called a trinity in names and numbers but a unity in nature, and nature secured the unity while need secured the trinity. How, then, did need not compel nature? And if need compelled nature, how is that which is compelled God? But if it did not compel nature, how did need secure the trinity of names? 7. Suppose the need that gives rise to the Trinity comes from matter, and, as you hold, whatever comes into being is traced back through the chain of consequences to the first cause. How, then, will matter not be the cause of the Trinity? But if the need that accounts for the Trinity does not come from matter, tell us where that need comes from. 8. If God is sinless in every way, but the soul is not sinless in every respect, how is the soul the same as God? And if nothing that is sinless in its essence becomes otherwise contrary to its nature, how has the soul, which is sinless in its essence, become sinful contrary to its nature? 9. If the Manichaeans are saved by knowledge and faith, what need do they have of the seal with oil? And if those who have knowledge and faith but still need the seal with oil can be saved, how can those who come to baptism with water in faith and knowledge not be saved? 10. Suppose all divine souls are equally good by the definition of their essence, and the definition of their essence admits neither subtraction nor addition. Then first, how do the Manichaeans become good through virtue? And second, if a soul in some way becomes evil after being good, how does it not lose the essence it had before? For in their view good and evil are essences. 11. The divine Scriptures transfer the term "death" from the natural death of the body to immortal souls that have died, contrary to their nature, in their transgressions. How, then, do they not transfer the name "resurrection" from the natural resurrection of the dead to immortal souls? For in the metaphors used in teaching, the reality of the things from which the metaphor is taken comes first. And if Jesus never draws a metaphor from things that never happen in nature, how, on your view, did he transfer the term "resurrection" to souls from a resurrection of the dead

that never happens at all? 12. Was Jesus speaking truly when he called himself the Son of Man? If he was not speaking truly when he called himself the Son of Man, how was he speaking truly when he called himself the Son of God? But if he spoke truly in calling himself both, how is he not both? 13. If Jesus did well to follow Jewish custom in some matters when he taught people, how is his Father not good, who followed the custom of the ancients and trained the Hebrews in piety? And if, setting aside the childishness of those who needed such things, the rest of the Old Testament is very good, how does the Old Testament not belong to the good God? 14. The Manichaeans say that the divine essence, that is, the soul that comes from the divine essence, must be handed over to eternal punishment for sins committed under necessity. If they are not mistaken in this, how are the children of truth mistaken when they say that those who were made by God but sinned of their own free will must be punished? And if it is just to say that the punishment of evil comes to an end, how is it unjust to say that the punishment of souls and bodies comes to an end? 15. If coming into being is evil, how is decay not good? And if growth is wicked, how is diminishing not good? And if decay is evil, how is coming into being not good? And if diminishing is wicked, how is growth not good? And if it is possible for coming into being and decaying, growing and diminishing, which are contrary to one another in essence, to be something evil, tell us why it is not possible for both the good and the evil to be praiseworthy in some respect. 16. Suppose the divine soul, while it is in a body, is bound by two bonds: one is the incorporeal evil that naturally clings to bodies, the other is the body itself. And suppose it is more bearable to be bound by one bond than by two, as experience bears out. How, then, are those who kill irrational animals, and who cut people down like plants, not doing a good deed? For they free the soul from one bond and its hardship. And if the soul is bound to matter, then first, how did it come to matter and put on its opposite as a bond [?]? And second, how is it bound to a body by necessity when it is simple in its essence? For everything that is simple in its essence is free from the bond of necessity. On these matters I await your answer.

On What Is Truly Good

In God the good is his essence. In created things it is an activity directed toward what lies outside them. It is an accident, attained through action or contemplation. Human beings living in the flesh attain the good through action, and the intellectual powers attain it through contemplation and prayer. Since, then, the good is an accident in created things, in them being certainly also comes first

Every activity has its being in coming to be. It does not exist before the motion, that is, the action, of the one who acts, nor does it remain after the motion. Often only the finished product is left behind as a reminder of the action. Activity, then, is action, and every action is the action of some essence and does not exist without an essence.

On Evil

The word "evil" has two meanings: sometimes it signifies affliction, sometimes sin. In the proper sense, sin is evil. Affliction is called evil only by a loose use of the word. For affliction is not altogether evil, and it often brings about salvation, whether it comes as some natural disease or as some outside mishap that befalls us and does us harm. If these things were evils in the proper sense, and not rather instruments of correction devised by God's providence to bring people to their senses, they would never be the cause of any good. But as it is, the very expectation of them often restrains [?] people who easily slip into sin and makes them fear God, and it wards off the harm that comes from these things [?]. It rouses us to entreat God, whether what we expect is a wild beast or a snake, war or famine, some illness, or slander and plotting contrived by people's wicked will. Slander and plotting are properly affliction: for the one who commits them they are sin, but for the one who suffers them they are not evil in the proper sense. They are not altogether evils. On the contrary, for those who are courageous in God's sight they bring the greatest renown among people, and they store up for them benefits and eternal rewards with God. So let no one be deceived into calling afflictions evils in the proper sense. For if what afflicts is evil, and not rather a means of correction that calls us to righteousness and every virtue, then let no one beat his son when he does wrong. Let no one praise a person entrusted with office who condemns a robber to the sword, or confirms by judicial sentence that he be handed over to the beasts to be devoured. Let no one praise a physician who cuts away a festering sore with the knife, for he afflicts his patient. Let no one allow theriac to be compounded from vipers, if indeed the Manichaeans say that snakes are evil. But those who ignorantly revile these things do not know

that everything is good that lacks nothing for the purpose for which God made it. How, then, are these things not very good, even if some of them are not substances and merely befall us because of natural weakness? Of natural things, some come about by the necessity of nature. By "the necessity of nature" I mean the things that nature brings about on its own and against our will, such as dying, and a living being growing up to its appointed age. Others come about as nature takes its course, yet they may also not happen, such as begetting children through intercourse. This belongs to what is contingent, since intercourse is not always followed by the begetting of children. All the things that happen by the necessity of nature come about without sin, even [?] in human beings, who are governed by reason. The things that may or may not happen are blameless in irrational nature, whatever their activity may be, for these creatures do not have reason by nature to weigh what ought to be done. But in human beings, who are governed by reason, these things are sometimes evils in the proper sense: when right reason does not guide the action, because it has been weakened by our sloth or wholly crippled by our pleasures. For sin is the choice and use, by rational beings acting irrationally, of things that by nature may either happen or not. Human virtue is being able to do something and to be stirred by natural impulse, yet, if it would be improper [?] to do it, to refrain from such actions with reason as one's helmsman, and to trample on the bait of pleasure.

But they say: "Why did God not make us incapable of sinning, so that we would not sin willingly?" Those who put forward such objections seem to resent that God did not make them stones and logs. They seem to blame their Benefactor for making human beings rational, and not rather unable to move toward a choice between good and evil. And if they say, "We should have been made rational and able to know good and evil, but unchangeable in doing good," they seem to me to be asking for nothing other than that we should not have become human beings at all, but should be of the same nature as God. For God alone is incapable of committing true wickedness. That is why the Apostle says, "Since it is impossible for God to lie." For wickedness is a kind of weakness found in created beings, but what trace of weakness can there be in the uncreated? And if we were of the same nature as God, we would no longer be creatures, but gods by nature, just as he is God.

On Darkness

Darkness, then, should be defined as a lightlessness of the air, which exists through the privation of light and not as a substance; or as a place shaded by an obstructing body [?]. Simply put, it is a place deprived of light.
